The effects of the coronavirus will weigh on economic activity in the near term and pose risks to the economic outlook. Consistent with Bagehot’s lender-of-last-resort doctrine and Goodfriend (2002) on modern operating frameworks (interest on reserves and standing facilities), the FOMC cut the policy rate to 0–0.25 percent, set IOR at 0.10 percent, expanded repo operations, and initiated large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS, alongside U.S. dollar swap lines to ease global funding strains. Theory and evidence on forward guidance and inflation-forecast targeting (Svensson and Woodford, 2005) imply these steps can stabilize expectations and compress term premia, supporting credit flows; however, literature also finds QE’s real-economy impact can be limited at the zero lower bound. Balancing these insights, near-term risks are significant but partly offset by the policy backstops.
